title: The sky folded into brass
note: The astrolabe folded the whole sky onto one brass plate, and turning its star map could read the hour, the prayer times and the latitude.

research.retell: An astrolabe is a brass model of the sky where you sight a star, turn its star map to match, and read off the time, the prayer times and your location, and one of its tenth century makers was a woman named in a single line of an old book catalogue.
proof: An astrolabe is the sky folded into a brass plate. / kept it the working computer of educated people for a thousand years.

In the catalogue of books he compiled at Baghdad around 987, Ibn al-Nadim lists the makers of astrolabes, and among them names the daughter of al-Ijli ... worked at the court of Sayf al-Dawla in Aleppo. [lights/all.json: al-ijliyya-astrolabe-maker]
Sight a star along the bar, read its height on the rim.
read its height on the rim [heroes.html] / a graduated rim [svg title]
then turn the rete, the pierced star map, until the brass sky matches the one overhead. / a turning star map [svg title]
find the times of prayer, take a latitude / the hour of the day / the times of prayer [svg labels]
The Greeks conceived it; Muslim instrument makers perfected it, adding interchangeable plates for different latitudes.
Every star map app on a phone is an astrolabe reborn, the folded sky turned from brass to glass.
Everything we securely know of her fits in one line of the Fihrist, the great tenth century catalog of Ibn al-Nadim.
